newsitem.title: USA: Stronger dollar buoyed by rate hopes at U.S. noon.
newsitem.headline: Stronger dollar buoyed by rate hopes at U.S. noon.

text.p: The dollar stood higher at midday after news of robust economic growth in the first quarter heightened expectations for another Federal Reserve interest rate hike, but talk of options-related selling limited the greenback's rise versus the yen, experts said.
The economy is running at a "fairly rapid" pace and the interest rate story is supporting the dollar, said David Gilmore, a partner at Foreign Exchange Analytics.
U.S. Gross Domestic Product (GDP) grew in the first quarter at a 5.6 percent annualized pace, the largest rise since a 6.0 percent increase in the fourth quarter of 1987.

Not long after the GDP report was released, Commerce Department Undersecretary Everett Ehrlich told Reuters Financial Television that the economy "has a lot of momentum" and could grow around 3.0 percent in the second quarter.
He also said "inflation has to be a concern", but that he saw no real sign of imminent danger.
"If the Fed's looking for stable growth at 2.0 to 2.5 (percent), we're far exceeding that pace," Gilmore said.
"And, I think, we have to be anticipating at least two more quarter point moves between now and June," he added.
The dollar rose to 1.7320/30 marks and 126.90/95 yen at midday, up from 1.7270/80 marks and 126.77/82 yen at the open.

Shortly after midday, the dollar inched above 127 yen, a level that many market participants had been watching during the session. Traders cited talk of selling interest at 127 yen and just above that level.

"In dollar/yen, there is rumored to be very good selling interest at 127 the figure due to an option knock out above that level," said Edith Wolf, head of corporate sales at Credit Commerciale de France. "And they do not want it to break the 127 figure."

In addition, talk circulated in the market of "good interest" to sell dollars by Japanese players around 127.10/15 yen and also German exporter offers to sell at 1.7350 marks, according to Stephen Jury, chief dealer at Union Bank of Switzerland.

Despite the hopes for higher short-term interest rates, market participants gave short shrift to a news report stating that Federal Reserve Chairman Alan Greenspan had secured support from Fed Vice Chairman Alice Rivlin and Governor Laurence Meyer to hike rates again on May 20.
The Fed hiked the federal funds target rate by 25 basis points to 5.50 percent on March 25. Policymakers are slated to meet on May 20 and on July 1 and 2.
Elsewhere, the dollar rose to 1.4735/45 Swiss francs at midday from 1.4685/95 francs at the open. Sterling slid to $1.6202/12 from $1.6280/90.
The dollar was nearly unchanged at Canadian $1.3968/73 compared with C$1.3969/74.
The news report said Greenspan assured Rivlin and Meyer there will be no further increase at the July policymakers' meeting if they agreed to tighten credit in May.

According to the news report, Rivlin and Meyer had disagreed with the decision to hike the federal funds rate on March 25. The news report referred to a Washington-based newsletter as the source of the story.
"People just aren't taking it seriously because it doesn't seem to be Greenspan's style to make agreements on conditions for his rate hikes," Wolf said.
